item.text:
Below is a drafting review of the supplied text, not a prediction that any particular challenge would succeed. Some items are direct loopholes; others are enforcement gaps or litigation risks. Constitutional concerns should be reviewed by legislative counsel.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” permits fragmentation.** Companies could divide training among multiple runs, checkpoints, separately trained components, or successive updates, each below the threshold. The bill needs aggregation rules covering related training activities and systems.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—No express aggregation of post-training compute.** Fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, distillation, and other post-training processes might substantially increase capabilities without any individual run crossing the threshold. Specify which stages count and how their compute is combined.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Inference and system-level compute are omitted.** A below-threshold model could achieve much greater capabilities through extensive inference-time computation, tool use, or coordination with other models. Section 2(1)(B) might eventually capture it, but the compute-based definition does not.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Fixed compute threshold can become obsolete.** Algorithmic improvements could permit prohibited capabilities at much lower training compute. There is no mechanism to revise the threshold or supplement it with updated technical criteria.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is excluded.** “Greater than” leaves a system trained using exactly the threshold outside this prong. Use “at least” if that boundary is intended to be covered.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** The text does not explain how to count operations across different numerical precisions, sparse computation, specialized hardware, or unconventional computing methods. Disputes over measurement could undermine both compliance and enforcement.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—Coverage during training is unclear.** “A model trained using” the threshold quantity could be read as describing an already-trained model rather than an ongoing or planned training project. Clarify when the prohibition attaches and whether starting a project expected to exceed the threshold is unlawful.

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—“Secretary” is undefined.** Although Commerce appears elsewhere, nothing identifies which Secretary makes capability determinations. This creates avoidable uncertainty about authority and the validity of designations.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—Capability coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** A highly capable system below the compute threshold may remain outside the definition until the Secretary acts. There are no mandatory notification requirements or decision deadlines to close that window.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, comparison populations, and a defined task universe. Different interpretations could produce inconsistent coverage and fair-notice challenges.

11. **Section 2(1)(B)—Testing conditions are unspecified.** Coverage might differ depending on whether evaluators test a base model, a constrained product, or a system equipped with tools and additional compute. Companies could present artificially restricted configurations unless the bill specifies the capabilities and configurations to evaluate.

12. **Section 2(1)(B)—No designation procedures or legal consequences are specified.** The bill omits notice, evidence standards, publication, effective dates, review procedures, and treatment of modified systems. This invites administrative-law disputes and uncertainty over when conduct becomes punishable.

13. **Section 2(1)—“Model” and “system” are not defined consistently.** The compute prong covers a model, while the capability prong covers a system. Clarify coverage of ensembles, agents, copies, derivatives, merged models, and products incorporating covered components.

14. **Section 2(2)—The U.S.-person definition omits important entities and residents.** It does not expressly include lawful permanent residents, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions matter especially for conduct abroad.

15. **Sections 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign affiliates provide a potential offshore route.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company is not necessarily a “U.S. person,” and foreign employees working abroad may also fall outside coverage. The bill lacks controlled-affiliate and anti-circumvention provisions, although direct development by the U.S. parent could still violate it.

16. **Section 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** Operators cannot reliably determine which chips count, and companies could dispute coverage based on chip specifications or marketing labels. A technical definition and an updating mechanism are needed.

17. **Section 2(3)—The facility threshold invites physical fragmentation.** Operators could distribute computing across multiple facilities, each containing 50,000 or fewer qualifying chips. There is no aggregation rule for commonly controlled sites or coordinated computing clusters.

18. **Section 2(3)—Chip count is a weak and static proxy for computing capacity.** Fewer, more powerful chips—or hardware outside the undefined chip category—could support very large training workloads without triggering registration. Coverage should account for computing capacity and technological change.

19. **Section 2(3)—Facility boundaries are unclear.** “Data center” and “containing” do not specify whether a campus, building, leased suite, or interconnected cluster is the relevant unit. Operators could structure leases or site boundaries to contest registration.

### Prohibition and exemptions

20. **Section 3(a)—Prohibited activities are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” leave uncertainty about research, testing, copying, maintenance, operation, and use of an existing system. Definitions should distinguish prohibited conduct from any intended permitted activities.

21. **Section 3(a)—Transfers and access are not expressly prohibited.** The bill does not expressly address selling or distributing model weights, importing systems, licensing access, or exporting covered technology. Some conduct might constitute development or deployment, but explicit coverage would avoid reliance on disputed interpretations.

22. **Section 3(a)—Enabling conduct is not expressly addressed.** Providing compute, financing, infrastructure, or technical support to a prohibited project may not itself constitute training, development, or deployment. Criminal aiding-and-abetting law may cover some knowing assistance, but it does not supply a complete civil anti-evasion regime.

23. **Section 3(a)—Territorial application to remote activity is unclear.** It is uncertain how the prohibition applies when customers, personnel, servers, and corporate entities occupy different countries. Specify the relevant jurisdictional connections for remote development and deployment.

24. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering is permanent and covers more than completed systems.** Merely beginning training before enactment exempts the system from the entire prohibition, including later development and deployment. A company could start numerous projects before enactment and continue them indefinitely.

25. **Section 3(b)—“Training began” has no substantive minimum.** A token training step could potentially establish grandfathered status. The bill needs an objectively verifiable cutoff and rules against nominal or sham starts.

26. **Section 3(b)—The identity of a grandfathered system is undefined.** Companies could claim that extensive retraining, new versions, derivatives, or merged systems are continuations of an exempt system. Specify which changes terminate the exemption.

27. **Section 3(b)—No process verifies grandfathering claims.** There is no required notice, contemporaneous documentation, or express allocation of the burden of establishing an exemption. Enforcement could depend on records held exclusively by the company claiming it.

28. **Section 3(c)—The safety-evaluation exemption is unrestricted.** It exempts “activities” without limiting their scale, duration, participants, or deployment conditions. Companies could characterize continued training or development as necessary to evaluate safety.

29. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The text does not say whether safety evaluation must be the sole or primary purpose. Commercial development with an asserted safety component could claim the exemption.

30. **Section 3(c)—No authorization or containment safeguards apply.** The exemption requires no advance approval, independent evaluator, security controls, reporting, or restrictions on releasing systems and weights. Even genuinely safety-oriented work could create or disseminate the prohibited capabilities.

### Registry and enforcement machinery

31. **Section 4(a)—Registration has no deadline or required contents.** Operators are not told when to register, what information to provide, or how to update ownership and capacity changes. This makes timely compliance difficult to enforce.

32. **Section 4(a)—“Operator” and geographic coverage are unspecified.** Responsibility is unclear among facility owners, lessees, cloud providers, and managers, and the bill does not state whether foreign facilities operated by U.S. persons must register. Clear allocation of duties is needed.

33. **Section 4(b)—Workload reporting is too vague.** “Describing” workloads does not expressly require compute totals, customer identities, related-run identifiers, model information, or records supporting exemptions. Superficial reports could satisfy the language while revealing little about prohibited activity.

34. **Section 4(b)—Quarterly reports may arrive too late.** A prohibited project could start and finish between reporting dates. The bill lacks advance notification and prompt reporting of threshold crossings or suspected violations.

35. **Sections 4–5—Registry violations have no express penalty.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. General false-statement law may apply to some deceptive submissions, but it does not cover every omission or compliance failure.

36. **Sections 2–5—No express rulemaking or lead enforcement authority.** The bill does not clearly assign implementation, investigations, administrative penalty assessments, or referrals to a designated agency. This leaves major procedural gaps and invites disputes about agency authority.

37. **Sections 2–5—No express access to evidence or verification powers.** There are no tailored record-retention duties, audit requirements, inspection powers, or administrative subpoena provisions. Existing investigative authorities may help, but the statute itself does not provide a coherent way to verify compute and capabilities.

38. **Sections 3–5—No express injunction or emergency-stop mechanism.** The bill specifies penalties but not a dedicated procedure to halt an ongoing training run or deployment promptly. It should authorize appropriate preventive relief rather than rely only on punishment after completion.

### Penalties and legal challenges

39. **Section 5(a)—The civil penalty may be an inadequate deterrent.** A maximum of $1 million per day could be treated as a business expense by a sufficiently large company, particularly for a short violation. There is no express revenue-based assessment or recovery of financial gains.

40. **Section 5(a)—The unit of violation is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether simultaneous projects, multiple systems, and separate acts generate separate daily penalties. Companies could argue that all unlawful activity on one day produces only one maximum penalty.

41. **Section 5(a)—Civil liability has no stated fault standard.** The provision does not specify whether liability is strict or requires knowledge or negligence. Combined with uncertain capability designations, this creates avoidable fair-notice disputes.

42. **Section 5(b)—“Willfully” may complicate criminal proof.** Courts could require proof that a defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, depending on the statutory context. Congress should specify the intended mental state for the conduct, coverage criteria, and exemption claims.

43. **Sections 2(1)(B), 3, 5(b)—Severe criminal penalties amplify vagueness concerns.** Undefined capability standards and broad activity terms are particularly problematic when violations carry ten years’ imprisonment. Clear statutory criteria and prospective notice would reduce due-process risk.

44. **Sections 3(a), 5—Research and dissemination restrictions could face First Amendment challenges.** Depending on how “develop” and “deploy” are interpreted, the prohibition could reach publication of code, weights, or scientific findings. The statute should clearly distinguish regulated conduct from protected expression and develop a record supporting any speech-related restrictions.

45. **Sections 2(1)(B), 3—Broad designation discretion invites delegation challenges.** The Secretary can trigger substantial prohibitions under a loosely specified capability standard. A challenge is not necessarily successful, but clearer criteria and procedural constraints would strengthen the law.

46. **Section 3(a)—The constitutional basis and jurisdictional scope are underdeveloped.** The text contains no express commerce nexus or findings explaining its reach over purely local, noncommercial activity and U.S. persons abroad. Congress may have relevant powers, but legislative counsel should ensure the prohibition is grounded and drafted accordingly.

47. **Act-wide—There is no severability provision.** If a court invalidates a definition, exemption, or application, the text gives no express direction to preserve the remainder. Severability language would reduce, though not eliminate, the risk of a broader invalidation.

### International agreement, duration, and timing

48. **Section 6—The international obligation requires effort, not an agreement.** “Seek to negotiate” does not require concluding an agreement, securing participation, or achieving implementation. The 18-month deadline is also unclear about whether it governs starting negotiations or attaining a negotiated outcome.

49. **Section 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions could reproduce domestic loopholes.** An agreement equivalent to section 3 could retain broad grandfathering and safety-evaluation exceptions. The provision specifies no verification, enforcement, anti-circumvention, or implementation requirements.

50. **Section 7(a)—The safety finding lacks a substantive standard.** “Can be developed safely” does not define acceptable risk, required evidence, or whether the finding must cover all covered systems rather than one safe development method. A narrow demonstration could be invoked to justify ending a much broader prohibition.

51. **Section 7(a)—The National Academies report is unspecified.** No provision commissions or funds the report or defines its scope, methods, independence safeguards, or required conclusions. Nor is Congress expressly required to find that the report supports lifting the prohibition.

52. **Section 7(a)—The legal status of remaining provisions after lifting the prohibition is unclear.** The text says section 3’s prohibition ends, but does not clearly address pending cases, accrued penalties, or how the registry and treaty mandate should operate afterward. Express transition and savings rules would prevent disputes.

53. **Section 7(b)—The sunset defeats the safety-based duration rule.** The entire Act expires after ten years regardless of whether Congress finds development safe. Companies could wait out the prohibition without satisfying section 7(a).

54. **Section 7(b)—Expiration also eliminates supporting machinery.** The sunset reaches registration and reporting duties, not just the prohibition. Express savings and transition provisions should clarify treatment of pending proceedings, existing records, and outstanding obligations.

55. **Sections 5(a), 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while the Act does not take effect for 180 days. This creates an apparent invitation to impose penalties for conduct before the prohibition is operative and should be reconciled expressly.

56. **Sections 3(b), 8—The 180-day delay permits a rush of otherwise prohibited activity.** Companies can train or deploy during the gap before the prohibition takes effect, although projects begun after enactment would not qualify for grandfathering. Immediate interim restrictions or reporting requirements would close that window.
